subject: english
outcomes: Use appropriate language to dramatise short plays
contentSummary:  Introduction: A short play is a form of drama that tells interesting stories within a limited timeframe. 
learnerActivities: Discussing basic elements of a short play
teachingMaterials:  Character Charts: with names of characters in the play
assessmentCriteria: Language to dramatise short plays used appropriately
exercises: Written Assessment (Quiz/Tests):
 Evaluate learners’ understanding of the basic elements of the play through
individual written responses by administering a written quiz or a set of open-
ended questions. These may include:
Closed Questions:
Multiple-choice or true/false questions about the characters, plot, or setting.
Example: “Who says the lines, ‘My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready
stand...’?”
Open-Ended Questions:
Questions that require learners to explain concepts in depth.
Example: "How does the dialogue between Romeo and Juliet in this scene
demonstrate their developing relationship?"

contentSummary:  Introduction: Listening comprehension is the ability to understand spoken information. In this lesson, learners will practise listening carefully to passages and identifying key ideas. This skill is essential for following instructions, engaging in conversations, and acquiring new knowledge. 

Discussing the Passages

assessmentCriteria: Information listened to and comprehended correctly.
exercises:  Practical Demonstration: Observe how well learners re-tell the story in their groups.
 Written Assessment: Observe how learners participate in the given assignment and
whether they are able to listen to information and comprehend correctly.

subject: english
outcomes: Write a description of an animal.
contentSummary:  Introduction: Descriptive composition involves painting a vivid picture of a subject using detailed language. When describing an animal, the aim is to capture its appearance, behaviour, and unique traits to engage the reader's senses. The main focus is on describing an animal's physical features, movements, sounds, and habitat. The goal is to create a clear, engaging image of the animal that allows readers to connect with it through rich, sensory details. 2.1.
learnerActivities: Reading model descriptive compositions on animals.
Discussing features of a descriptive composition
Using appropriate descriptive language
Writing short descriptive compositions of animals.
teachingMaterials:  A sample description of an animal
assessmentCriteria: Description of an animal written correctly.
exercises:  Learners choose an animal (either familiar or exotic) and write a detailed description
focusing on sensory details like appearance, behaviour, and habitat
 Learners write short descriptions on given topics (Describe including physical traits,
sounds, movements, and personal impressions to engage the reader).

subject: english
outcomes: Use adverbs in different positions in sentences.
learnerActivities: Discussing the Different Kinds of Adverbs
Using Adverbs in Different Positions in Sentences
teachingMaterials:  Sentence strips with incomplete sentences for learners to complete with adverbs.
 Black/Whiteboard for demonstrating how word order changes in a sentence.
 Handouts with sentences for learners to rearrange
assessmentCriteria: Adverbs in different positions in sentences used appropriately.
exercises:  Observation: Teacher observes learners as they classify adverbs and
provide examples, checking for understanding of each adverb's type
(place, time, frequency, manner, degree).
 Questioning: Ask learners to give additional examples of each type of
adverb and explain their function in the sentence. This will help gauge
whether they can identify adverbs correctly.
 Learner Review: During group work, learners can review each other’s
classifications of adverbs to promote collaborative learning and correct
any misunderstandings.
 Quiz on Adverbs: Make sure learners understand the multiple-choice and
fill-in-the-blank questions are based on the lesson's content.

contentSummary:  Introduction: A sentence summary condenses the original material into a single, concise sentence that communicates the main idea or purpose of the content. It serves as a brief overview, providing a snapshot of the content in just a few words or a single sentence, while still capturing the essence of the original material. When writing a sentence summary, the goal is to highlight the most important points and ideas without getting bogged down in excessive detail. This practice is useful for quickly understanding and recalling key concepts.
learnerActivities: Reading the Given Summary Passage (Paragraph)
choosing the best sentence summary for a given paragraph
Supplying the best Sentence Summary
exercises:  Ask learners to pair up and share their sentence summaries with each other.
 Encourage learners to give constructive feedback on how well the sentence
captures the core message of the paragraph.
 Encourage learners to practise writing sentence summaries for other passages as a
way of improving their comprehension and synthesis skills.
Home work:
 Give worksheets with paragraph texts and ask learners to read and make sentence
summaries.

contentSummary:  Introduction: Extensive reading can be defined as reading done for pleasure or gaining general understanding by focusing on a large volume of materials. contentSummary:  Introduction: A paragraph summary is a concise restatement of the key points of a passage. It preserves the original content of the passage without including unnecessary details, examples, or repetitions Summarising is an important skill that can improve reading comprehension and writing. By learning how to summarise paragraphs, we can better understand and communicate the core message of a text. This topic will focus on identifying the main idea, distinguishing important supporting details, and creating a concise summary that reflects the original passage’s meaning. 
learnerActivities: Reading given passage(s)
Choosing the best paragraph summary
exercises:  Teacher to ask learners to continue practising how to choose the paragraph by applying

contentSummary:  Introduction: Reciting poems is more than just reading words aloud. It is about bringing the poem to life with your voice, feelings, and expressions so that the listener can feel the message and emotion behind the lines. Through poetry recitation, people learn to speak clearly, use the right tone, and connect with the audience. In this topic, learners will explore how to use voice, facial expressions, and gestures to recite a poem effectively. Learners will practise how to recite a poem with confidence and expression. 
learnerActivities: Identifying appropriate elements to recite simple poems
Using appropriate expressions to recite poems on different cross-cutting
exercises:  Observe learners’ participation in discussions and recitation.
 Provide feedback on pronunciation, expression, and clarity.
 Ask oral questions and encourage class discussion on identifying the appropriate
elements of a poem (mood, tone).
 Ask learners to recite given poems and recognise rhythm and rhyme.
